newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Coffee grading row sparks rethink at LIFFE.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Coffee grading row sparks rethink at LIFFE.

text.p: The London Financial Futures Exchange (LIFFE) has agreed to review its new but tough robusta coffee quality-grading criteria which have come under renewed fire from traders.
Traders had in December protested against the changes in grading methods which they said caused them heavy financial losses.

The row reignited this month after more than 70 percent of coffee samples that were graded under the new criteria, which come into effect with the July contract onwards, failed the rigorous quality test and were thus rendered untenderable.
"People were hoping to make a profit if the coffee passed the grading. Now it hasn't, people are crying," said one trader.
On Wednesday LIFFE sent a circular to members spelling out the terms of reference for the review. But it stressed that it was likely to be several months before the results of the review were known.
In the meantime, it would continue to grade all coffee samples against the current quality terms.
Backers of the plan say that it would be unfortunate if LIFFE were to loosen the rules.
"Ultimately, it is a good thing, it pushes back to the quality standards in the origins," said one. "But any change on the terminal market is always very difficult."
The change in the grading rules was announced by the then-London Commodity Exchange in March 1996 after a consultation with the market.
The changes take effect with the July 1997 delivery contract onwards. All previously graded coffee would have to be re-graded for deliveries, an exercise which incurs additional costs.
The re-grading ruling has also incurred the wrath of major traders. In essence, some 24,000 tonnes of coffee that had received LIFFE quality certification must be regraded.

"This is an extraordinary move and in spite of remonstrations by the trade has been upheld," said one trader. The May contract, which was traded a premium, sank to a $100 discount to July when the LIFFE issued the ruling in December.

"One rule that has always been sacrosanct in the futures markets has been that the value of any trading position will not be tampered with. From what has happened here, what are we to expect in the future?" the trader asked.

The changes relate to the adjustments of bands of defects and the allowances awarded with regard to defects, the introduction of a moisture tolerance for deliverable coffee, and the introduction of a specific defect count of 50 for mouldy beans.
The moisture tolerance criterion was subsequently suspended until an appropriate method has been found to test for this requirement.
But the main complaint revolves around the introduction of a defect count for mouldy beans.
Under the old rules, examination for mould was a subjective process, but the new rules have introduced a measure of objectivity.
Traders said the new grading criteria had resulted in an alarmingly high failure rate of 72 percent this month. The overall failure rate was around 47 percent in May.
LIFFE said in the circular that the new rules were introduced to reflect the changes in the underlying physical market, widen the bands of acceptable coffee and increase the delivery base.

It said it was very important to treat mould as a serious defect in order to take full account of the growing concern relating to the level of ochrotoxins -- micro-organisms which in turn have been linked to the development of cancer -- contained in coffee mould.
